entries.title: Pumpkin Patches and Rom-Coms: How the Commanders Moved Past Sunday’s Tie
entries.summary: After their frustrating tie with the Giants, Washington’s players did their best to put it out of their minds and focus on Monday’s matchup with the 49ers.
entries.content:
Amik Robertson was not in a good mood after the Commanders’ 27-27 tie with the Giants on Sunday.

The cornerback was penalized three times, including a ticky-tacky defensive pass interference call that wiped out an interception he got late in the third quarter. “Bullshit,” was how he described the call.

But days later, Robertson felt much better and had since moved on from the Meltdown in Maryland. And what helped the 28-year-old Lousisana native get past that game?

Rom-coms, of course.

“I didn't want to watch ‘The Notebook,’” Robertson said. “I watched ‘Anyone But You.’”

The Giants game was a major letdown for Washington. They led by 14 points with just over 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter, and after getting in field goal range late in overtime, the Commanders let time run out in the game before they could even attempt the game-winning kick.

Head coach Dan Quinn called the tie “gutting.” Pro Bowl receiver Terry McLaurin said it stung. And star quarterback Jayden Daniels, who laid on the ground for crucial seconds on the final play, said the result sucked.

The team gave themselves a day to sit with the result, and after two days off ahead of a Monday Night Football matchup with the undefeated 49ers, they were eager to put Sunday’s tie behind them and move on to Week 6.

Each player had his own unique way of using the time off to help move on from one of the most disastrous endings in franchise history.

For some, their reprieve was television.

Robertson normally plays the Madden video game series in his free time, but it's hard to not think about football when you’re playing a football game. So he opted for the Glen Powell- and Sydney Sweeney-led “Anyone But You” to relax his mind.

Defensive lineman Deatrich Wise also uses television to relax. But when you have a 3-year-old son, you tend to have little control over the remote.

“Paw Patrol, Sesame Street, stuff like that,” Wise said of his off-day viewing habits. “Monster Jams. It’s usually what it is.”

Linebacker Kain Medrano visited a pumpkin patch in Frederick County, Maryland, with his girlfriend, who he said “gets very festive” during this time of year. It was an opportunity to give attention to something other than his job for the first time in weeks.

“You give football a break for a quick second, just focus on family, on stuff that you don't really get to focus on day in, day out,” said Medrano. “Just because you're here in the facility all the time.”

Spending time with loved ones was a common thread for other players.

Linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson said his 3-year-old daughter provides both an escape from football and the perspective that you don’t have to linger on the negative results.

“Being with my daughter, she don't really give me time to sit and sulk about the football games,” Chaisson said. “I'm coming home and trying to just break everything down and cleanse my mind of it, and she jumps right on my lap. She don't care about the outcome of the game. She wants to go outside, draw chalk on the ground and play hopscotch, whatever it may be.”

Receiver Treylon Burks shares two daughters with his wife, Shelby. He used his time away from the facility to be with them. That said, the Arkansas native has other hobbies he would’ve liked to partake in, but the topography of the D.C. area makes it a bit difficult.

“It ain't much hunting and fishing out here for me, so I'll just wait till I can get back home to do that,” he said.

As reassuring and supportive as family can be, the pain of defeat (or a tie) can be an itch they can never scratch. Left tackle Brandon Coleman spent time with his girlfriend, family and friends, but he couldn’t stop replaying Sunday’s game in his head.

“They try to distract, but at the end of the day we're all competitors,” Coleman said. “It's tough — especially from something like that — to not think about it and have those thoughts after a game.”

Quinn implored the team to take those feelings and apply them to the final 12 games of the season. While a letdown like Sunday could tear a team apart, Quinn believes the adversity they’ve faced this season can help.

“We identified we only played 30% of the season,” Quinn said. “There's so much that's in front of us, and it's going to be an absolute battle.”

For what felt like the first time in his three-year career, Daniels faced heavy criticism for his decision-making in the Giants game. No matter what happened leading up to the final play, it was Daniels who took the sack and laid on the ground with no urgency.

"Jayden Daniels probably cost my man Dan Quinn his job, to be honest with you," Packers linebacker Micah Parsons said on his podcast this week.

Daniels said he leaned on his circle, including his parents, to move past the result. But more importantly, the 2024 Rookie of the Year award winner got back to work. He lifted weights, watched the Giants film and then got a jump start on studying the 49ers defense.

This may have been the lowest moment of his young career, but Daniels understands that dwelling on the tie or what he could have done differently won’t magically change the team’s 1-3-1 record.

“You still think about stuff like that, right?” he said. “But it can't help me. It can help me moving forward … I can't dwell on the past too much, because I got a game on Monday night to worry about.”

entries.title: Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions, Citing National Interest
entries.summary: Named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill had sought to clamp down on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
entries.content:
By Will Weissert and Meg Kinnard

President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy

Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.

His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.

The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.”

The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.

Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin

Under last week's agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.

The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.

Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day." In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed.

She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it.

“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Health Officials: DOGE Disruptions Upended $112 Million Epidemiology Contract
entries.summary: The NIH gave a no-bid extension to a health care company after DOGE scrambled plans for open competition.
entries.content:
Last year, the National Institutes of Health was preparing to allow health care companies to compete for a multimillion-dollar follow-on to a decade-old contract funding epidemiological studies.

A “full and open competition” was the NIH’s plan when a 10-year, $112 million contract awarded to Social & Scientific Systems Inc. in June 2016 was nearing its expiration.

The government typically prefers to solicit bids from multiple potential contractors when such a need arises so that healthy competition can keep costs down.

But the Department of Government Efficiency got in the way.

“Although planning for the recompete was underway in calendar year 2025 … Establishing and Implementing the President’s ‘Department of Government Efficiency’ caused unforeseen circumstances beyond the control of the acquisition office causing significant delays to the acquisition process,” an NIH spending document obtained by The Washington Sun reads.

“Between 2025 and 2026, several delays occurred due to staffing changes, organizational transition and other internal realignments,” the document continues.

As a result, instead of the “full and open competition” the agency had hoped for, it handed Social & Scientific Systems Inc. a two-year, no-bid, $20 million extension to its current work to carry out “research on the effects of the environment on human health.”

“Unfortunately, all efforts made to recompete are out of date and need to be updated and resubmitted for reviews,” the document reads. “The current recompetition has not yet begun and requires full two years to ensure proper attention is made to the process to satisfy acquisition rules, regulations and guidelines.”

The NIH noted that if it were to switch awardees now, the “costs associated with transition are estimated at approximately $9 Million.”

The document itself received sign-offs from NIH officials in April and June when the contract was extended, but it was only posted to a government website this week.

DOGE, the brainchild of Elon Musk and President Donald Trump, set out to revolutionize what the pair viewed as a woefully inefficient federal bureaucracy. Instead, DOGE’s chaotic implementation sometimes resulted in a breakdown of agency action meant to reduce taxpayer spending.

The NIH did not return a request for comment.
entries.author: Mark Alfred

entries.title: Lawmakers Outraged With Trump's Decision to Waive Russian Sanctions
entries.summary: It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington.
entries.content:
By Lisa Mascaro

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.

Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

“Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”

Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and “not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.

Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions.

The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington.

Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law

It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine.

But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago.

Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday.

Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern.

Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal.

New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump's diesel deal with Putin. “At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement.

He called the deal “corrupt” and said it “goes against everything the United States stands for.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Maryland Loses to Rutgers, 37-30
entries.summary: Losing to Rutgers on Homecoming in front of a sparse crowd is about as bad as it gets.
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

COLLEGE PARK,Md. (AP) — KJ Duff caught two touchdown passes — including one with a spectacular one-handed grab — and Rutgers held on for a 37-30 victory over Maryland on Saturday.

The Terrapins (2-5, 0-4 Big Ten) have lost five in a row, and they blew a 10-point halftime lead in this matchup between embattled coaches Mike Locksley of Maryland and Greg Schiano of the Scarlet Knights. Duff caught nine passes for 113 yards, and Clay Thevenin scored both a rushing touchdown and a receiving one as Rutgers (2-4, 1-2) rallied in the final two quarters.

Antwan Raymond’s 2-yard TD run gave the Scarlet Knights a 37-23 lead with 4:03 left in the fourth quarter. Malik Washington’s second touchdown pass of the game, a 10-yarder to DeJuan Williams, brought Maryland back within seven with 2:17 to play.

After a false start on fourth-and-1 from its own 34, Rutgers had to punt, giving Maryland the ball with 1:52 remaining. The Terps reached the Rutgers 11, but Williams dropped a pass in the flat that would have been an easy first down — and maybe a TD — and on fourth-and-2, Washington's pass to Dorian Fleming in the back corner of the end zone was ruled incomplete with 16 seconds left.

A replay showed Fleming's toe appearing to be on the sideline as he made the catch, and the call stood.

With the Terps up 7-0, Dylan Lonergan lofted a pass to the left side of the end zone toward Duff. He was able to catch the ball with his right hand while landing his right foot inbounds. He was so off balance that his left foot was up around his head.

After that 15-yard touchdown catch, Duff added a 9-yarder in the second quarter, but Maryland's Trey Reddick blocked the extra point, and Jamare Glasker ran it back to give the Terrapins two points and a 16-13 lead.

Chris Durr Jr. scored on a 16-yard reverse to give the Terps a 23-13 halftime lead, but Maryland fell apart after that. Sean O'Haire missed a third-quarter field goal from 34 yards, and Lonergan found Thevenin for a 19-yard touchdown that tied it at 23. After the Terrapins went three-and-out, Thevenin gave Rutgers the lead with a 7-yard scoring run.

The takeaway

Rutgers: The Scarlet Knights beat an FBS opponent for the first time this season, and Duff earned himself a well-deserved highlight.

Maryland: Was this Locksley's last game at the helm? The Terps have an open date coming up, so if a change is going to be made during the season this might be the time. Losing to Rutgers on Homecoming in front of a sparse crowd is about as bad as it gets.

Up next

Rutgers: at Northwestern next Saturday.

Maryland: off next week before hosting Illinois on Oct. 31.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Capitals Beat Devils, 4-2
entries.summary: Ryan Leonard scored a highlight-reel goal.
entries.content:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Ryan Leonard scored a highlight-reel goal and the Washington Capitals beat the New Jersey Devils 4-2 on Saturday afternoon.

Ilya Protas, Dylan Strome and Boone Jenner also scored and Vincent Desharnais had two assists for the Capitals, who have won back-to-back games.

Arsenal Gritsyuk and Timo Meier scored for the Devils, who dropped to 4-4-0 to open the season.

The Devils got on the board first roughly halfway through the first period, when Gritsyuk beat Logan Thompson through traffic at the end of New Jersey’s second power play of the period.

With 3:18 to go in the first, though, Leonard would even the score and change the momentum with his spectacular goal. In the final seconds of Washington’s power play, Leonard took the puck up ice himself, going coast to coast before beating Luke Hughes, cutting to the inside and deking out Jake Allen for his third goal of the season.

From there, the Capitals took over the game, starting with back-to-back goals in a span of 4 minutes, 46 seconds to open the second period. First, Protas buried a cross-zone feed from Alex Ovechkin to give Washington the 2-1 lead. Then, Strome finished off a passing play from Alex Tuch and Jordan Kyrou to put Washington up by two.

Later in the frame, Jenner tucked in a point drive that bounced to the front for his fourth goal in five games, extending the lead to 4-1 going into the third.

New Jersey pushed hard in the third and pulled within two late when Meier scored with 18.4 seconds to go in regulation, but otherwise, Thompson shut them down with 29 saves on 31 shots to secure the win for the Capitals.

Allen had 21 saves in the loss for New Jersey.

Up next

Capitals: Host the Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday.

Devils: Return home to face the Colorado Avalanche on Tuesday.

entries.title: DOJ Asks a Judge to Recuse Herself From East Potomac Park Case
entries.summary: Government lawyers claim Reyes has overstepped her authority in the case.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is seeking to remove the judge presiding over the East Potomac Park case after she barred officials from removing more trees from the public golf course this week — asking that she be replaced with someone who doesn’t show “open hostility” toward the government.

Justice Department lawyers, in a motion filed Friday evening, are accusing U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes of unfairly questioning government attorneys’ intelligence, saying she allowed her disdain for the administration to influence how hearings unfold and had generally overstepped her authority.

Central to the escalating tensions is the administration’s decision last weekend to remove 430 healthy, non-invasive trees from the Washington, D.C., course, with plans to cut down more — despite government lawyers’ promise to provide the court ample notice before doing so.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Reyes issued a restraining order Monday after a four-hour hearing, during which Reyes excoriated the government for not giving notice and said the administration had lost all of its credibility in the case. She also requested an Interior Department official testify under oath in the case to determine if she’d been lied to during proceedings.

“On what universe did anyone in your office think that was acceptable?” Reyes asked a DOJ attorney.

The attorney responded, “Your honor, we did our best.”

“No, you did not do your best,” she replied. “You did your absolute worst.”

The DOJ accused Reyes of belittling and shouting at its attorney “in an unorthodox and regrettable show of judicial impropriety” requesting she recuse herself from the case.

During the hearing, the DOJ said Reyes’ behavior cast doubt on whether government attorneys can act in good faith after she at one point said “the government can’t be trusted,” according to the motion.

Plaintiffs issued a response to the DOJ motion later Friday in opposition to the attempt to remove Reyes from the case, saying the government’s filing had incorrectly summarized their position as against publicly releasing a recording of the hearing. They said they had no reason to believe Reyes should be recused from the case and added that they would be fine with releasing court audio.

In February, the D.C. Preservation League, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting historic spaces, sued the Interior Department, asking the court to bar the administration from conducting renovations on the East Potomac Park land for President Donald Trump’s golf course construction project.

During proceedings, government lawyers repeatedly assured the court they would provide advance notice of major developments that could affect the more than 100-year-old course. Reyes told the attorneys in May that “if anyone orders big things to show up, and by ‘big things,’ I mean anything, you know, more than my sedan — then I want plaintiffs to have notice.”

The government notified the court of the pending removal of 529 trees at 4:55 p.m. on Oct. 9, which would constitute around 13% of the site’s trees. Over the next two days, the government removed roughly 430 trees, “none of which were hazardous or posed safety concerns,” the temporary restraining order says.

In prior hearings, Reyes provided the government with “the benefit of the doubt” that it would not “act first and ask forgiveness later.”

In Friday’s motion, however, the government described her behavior as “nothing short of egregious.”

“Her misconduct in other high-profile litigation involving the Trump Administration only confirms that she cannot serve as an impartial arbiter of the issues in this case,” the motion, signed by Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr.

In March, Reyes blocked the Trump administration’s attempts to ban transgender people from military service, finding the policy would likely violate the Constitution.

Reyes would need to grant the motion to recuse herself. If she denies it, the Trump administration could ask the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals to intervene.

If approved, the case would be transferred to another judge.

Federal law requires judges to disqualify themselves from legal proceedings if it’s determined their “impartiality might reasonably be questioned,” the motion states.

“No reasonable observer could consider Judge Reyes sufficiently impartial to adjudicate this case,” Woodward wrote.

The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Monday, October 19.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: Spirit Beat Gotham, 1-0, in Crucial Win as Playoffs Approach
entries.summary: It was the first win for the Spirit (16-8-4) over Gotham since June 23, 2024.
entries.content:
By Phuoc Nguyen

Defender Lucia Di Guglielmo scored her first-ever National Women's Soccer League goal and the Washington Spirit clinched a playoff spot with 1-0 victory over Gotham on Saturday.

It was the first win for the Spirit (16-8-4) over Gotham since June 23, 2024.

The road loss at Audi Field denied Gotham (16-5-7) a chance to clinch the NWSL Shield and snapped a four-match unbeaten streak.

In the 70th minute, Spirit midfielder Mélissa Bethi delivered a pinpoint lob pass to Di Guglielmo. She snuck her shot past Gotham goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger for the lead and game-winner.

Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver made two saves for her 10th clean sheet of the season.

Midfielder Leicy Santos returned from injury and started for the Spirit in her first appearance since Aug. 8.

After her contract termination with the Chicago Stars, Gotham defender Leila Ouahabi started in her debut for her new club.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Appears to Have Dropped the ‘Military Complex’ Justification for His Arch
entries.summary: New plans released by the government do not mention snipers, drones or ammunition, as the president previously suggested.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump turned course last month when he said his proposed 250-foot arch would have a military complex attached. But new documents indicate that Trump’s security plans — which seemed to be a late addition meant to boost the project’s chances — are not part of the final plan.

Trump’s push to highlight the project’s military importance came as the arch drew deep scrutiny for its hefty multimillion-dollar price tag. However, plans published by the National Capital Planning Commission made no mention of defense facilities.

On Sept. 20, Trump said the military requested that the Memorial Circle project house a “top-grade military complex.” That proposal would have housed, stored and allowed use of large numbers of drones and snipers on both the roof and plaza areas, in addition to storing large quantities of sniper ammunition.

The final project plans, as published by the Interior Department, include construction of the Triumphal Arch’s associated plaza and landscape improvements, supporting utility and stormwater infrastructure, traffic and pedestrian circulation modifications, security features, lighting and temporary staging and laydown areas.

There are no indications the project will include military infrastructure based on the submitted details.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

In an emailed statement to The Washington Sun, the Interior Department said the arch’s current design is capable of accommodating the national security function mentioned in the president’s Truth Social post. The Pentagon referred The Washington Sun to the White House, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The DOI maintains the arch will enhance the visitor experience at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

The proposed concrete structure has drawn criticism from flight attendants and veterans, who warn it could pose safety risks to pilots and obstruct landmark views. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA denounced Trump’s plans, arguing the project would pose a threat to aviation safety.

The flight attendants’ union said the arch would interfere with planes’ final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and cited safety concerns stemming from the Jan. 29, 2025, crash in which an American Airlines commercial plane and an Army helicopter collided midair over the Potomac River, killing 67 people.

“DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path,” said the association’s president, Sara Nelson. “Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles, or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always.”

In a statement issued in September, the Federal Aviation Administration said the arch would not pose a safety hazard to aircraft.

Experts reviewed airspace, air traffic patterns and procedures around the airport, as well as operations at nearby military/public-use airports and found the arch would be appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed toward the arch to make it noticeable to pilots, the FAA said.

Despite promoting the project as a memorial to military service, three veterans have sued the Trump administration to bar it from erecting the arch without congressional approval, stating the “view of the Lincoln Memorial from Arlington House will be obscured, disrupting the historic and symbolic link between the two.”

The National Capital Planning Commission has scheduled a hearing on Nov. 5 to discuss the prospective arch.
